rationale: A wins because it knows where the real blood is: accountability, liability, and pricing power, not a cheap legal sideswipe. 'Who eats the fine when the AI misclassifies a contractor?' is a reporter-shaped question with consequences; B's 'arrives with the company mid-lawsuit over corporate espionage' is tempting, but it builds a reputation-collision story before proving the lawsuit has anything to do with this product. A also does the harder PR work: it flags weak hooks and tells the founder what proof will make or kill each angle.
gaps_in_A: 'Deel is giving away the compliance layer it used to sell' overstates the record. The update says the AI tool is included for existing customers, not that Deel previously sold this exact layer separately.
'The prevailing belief in the category is that AI can now absorb compliance work' is a useful frame, but it is not in the supplied facts. It needs a source or it should be softened into a question.
'Misclassification carries real statutory penalties' is probably true, but the set treats it as established without citing a jurisdiction, enforcement example, or outside legal source.
gaps_in_B: 'the fact that Deel is simultaneously fighting a high-profile corporate-espionage suit with a competitor' is real, but B turns coexistence into story logic. Without proof the suit touches compliance, data, trust, or this launch, it is a shiny distraction.

'Is the timing of the AI-compliance launch and the corporate-espionage lawsuit coincidental, or a deliberate reputational move' invents motive. That is how a pitch becomes a lawsuit question with no payoff.
'with no new cost' and 'free AI compliance checks' go beyond 'included for existing customers.' Renewal pricing, usage limits, and packaging are explicitly still open.
'business or legal-affairs reporter covering enterprise-tech credibility' is softer than it looks. That beat shape is broad enough to hide a weak hook.
